new_statements.rule_in_words: Moskona is described as a culminative pitch accent language (one high-toned accented syllable per word, other syllables low/neutral), not a stress language. Where placement is predictable, the accent sits on the penultimate syllable of the root, with only one accent per polysyllabic word; a subset of roots (many fused nominal compounds and grammatical/function words such as eda 'then', tina 'but', mida 'what', ogura 'no') have lexically fixed, contrastive placement, and some roots (e.g. rot 'about', ek 'see') carry no accent at all. Verbal prefixes and the circumfix are unaccented; the enclitic -i 'PROT' carries an accent while -o 'EMP' does not; reduplicants copy the root's accent. Appendix A p. 409 restates: placement on roots is 'generally predictable, typically occurring on the penultimate syllable of the word', and contrasts this with Meyah's contrastive placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; the source states 'only one fixed accent per polysyllabic word' (p. 51) and 'a single tonal contrast' (p. 49).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical (contrastive) accent placement in fused nominal forms and function words (pp. 52-53, exx. 122-123); unaccented roots (§2.3.2.1, p. 53); root-final /a/ elision in running speech with accent then on the final syllable (p. 5, 'the accent placement frequently shifts to the final syllable'); Holton & Klamer 2018:587 summarise this as 'a small number of polysyllabic words with ultimate stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Root/word level (accent on 'the penultimate syllable of the root'); running-speech forms retain the placement; prefixes and circumfix outside the accent domain; enclitic -i can attract the accent. The author labels the predictable pattern 'quantity-sensitive' but gives no explicit syllable-weight rule; her acoustic section (§2.3.1) shows pitch is the main correlate, with amplitude and (not always) duration. Note that extracted text dropped the acute accent marks on example words, so per-word placement in exx. 115-128 must be read from the PDF, not the.
new_statements.identity_note: Gravelle 2010 describes Moskona (mosk1236, ISO mtj), with most data from the northern (Moyeba) dialect; a southern (Meyerga) dialect differs only phonemically (§1.3.3, p. 9). Older sources (Voorhoeve; Reesink 2002 PL 524) treated Moskona as a dialect of Meyah (meya1236); Gravelle 2010 Appendix A p. 409 states that accent placement differs between the two (Moskona generally predictable penultimate, Meyah contrastive) and contributes to their lack of mutual intelligibility, so the Meyah pitch accent descriptions (Gravelle 2002 PL 524 pp. 121-123; Gravelle 2004) must not be used for Moskona.
